item.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
item.question: What is Freeman doing with the abalone shell behind the quartz crystal, and what is the general permission he draws from it?
item.answer: He is using defocus to strip an object of its identity and keep only its hue. The crystal is colourless but refracts, so he placed a polished abalone shell several inches behind it and shot at a fairly wide aperture — just enough to keep most of the crystal sharp. At that distance and blur the shell is made completely abstract and unrecognisable for what it was, present only as iridescent blue and green which the crystal's facets then refract. The general permission he states is that there are times when colour will enliven an image and times when it matters less what those colours actually represent in real life.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Complex Surfaces', the closing figure
item.question: The book says adding a three-dimensional object to a glossy flat surface both improves the picture and makes the lighting easier. Why does it help, and why does the chapter drop the idea immediately?
item.answer: It helps because the object's reflection in the surface is unambiguous evidence of gloss in a way that a featureless bright area is not: the reflection of a pair of eyeglasses in a polished lid tells the viewer the wood is glossy, and the authors say adding a secondary subject reveals the surface better than they are likely to render it alone. It makes the lighting easier for the same reason — the proof of the finish no longer has to be carried entirely by the shaped highlight. The chapter drops it because it had committed at the outset to two-dimensional and nearly two-dimensional subjects, and the authors say they cannot pursue the approach far without breaking that promise; three-dimensional subjects are the next chapter's business. So the claim is stated and demonstrated but deliberately not developed.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.question: "Black magic" in this book is not a figure of speech. What is it, and how is its hardness controlled?
item.answer: Black magic is anything added to a lighting set-up solely to place a black reflection in a metal surface. Its uses are practical: a black reflection in an edge helps differentiate that edge from the background, and reflected across the centre of a slightly irregular surface it adds dimension. It usually means a gobo, and its hardness is set by which side of the diffusion sheet the gobo sits on. Between the diffusion sheet and the subject, it makes a hard black reflection. Behind the sheet, away from the subject, it makes a softly graduated one, and the farther back it goes the softer it becomes. Where the source is an opaque reflector rather than a diffusion sheet a gobo cannot graduate, and the authors substitute a soft-edged stripe of black spray paint across the reflector.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'Black Magic', in the 'Other Resources' group, which gives the purpose, the gobo placement rule and the painted-stripe alternative.
confounders: assuming black magic means removing light, when its purpose is to place a specific dark shape
reversing the gobo rule — near the subject is hard, not soft
confusing it with a black card used as negative fill on a diffuse subject, which works by subtraction rather than by reflection

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Secondary Opaque Subjects'
item.question: A labelled glass bottle has to look premium and its label has to be legible. The lighting that gives the bottle its describing highlight puts a sheen across the paper. Work through the book's options and say which it rules out and why.
item.answer: The conflict is real and the book states it: most of a paper's reflection is diffuse but some is direct, so the light producing the direct reflection on the glass is also likely to obscure the label. Two remedies work. Move the offending light higher, so the label's direct reflection goes downward instead of toward the lens. Or, where good highlight placement forbids moving the light, interpose a small opaque card blocking exactly the angles that produce direct reflection on the label — and its size is critical: a gobo extending beyond the label's own family of angles will itself reflect in the glass. A polarizing filter is the third option and the book rules it out in most cases: much of the desirable highlight on the glass is usually polarized already, so a polarizer that eliminates the label's reflection is also likely to interfere with the light the glass needs. Underneath all three sits the prior question the authors insist comes first — which of the two is the principal subject — and they say that cannot be settled on a technical basis at all.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Secondary Opaque Subjects' for the three options and the gobo size constraint; 'Recognizing the Principal Subject' for the prior decision.

oversizing the gobo, which converts a label fix into a black reflection in the glass

source_terms: One of the first steps in lighting a scene is to look at the subject and decide what kind of reflection causes the subject to appear the way it does.
The next step is to position the light, the subject, and the camera to make the photograph capitalize on that type of reflection and minimize the others.
item.claim: The source's operative procedure has exactly two steps and a fixed order. First, look at the subject and decide which kind of reflection is responsible for how it looks. Second, position the light, the subject and the camera so that the photograph capitalizes on that reflection and minimizes the others. The source is explicit that "position the light" does not require a studio: choosing viewpoint, day and time outdoors performs the identical operation, and studio examples are used only because they are controllable enough to demonstrate the point.

mechanism.text: Because the surface determines the reflection type and the geometry determines whether the camera can see it, a lighting decision is made by first identifying the type and then arranging the geometry that admits it.

scope.conditions: any subject; the source claims the principles apply to any type of photography

caveats.text: builds directly on live chapter-3 knowledge — the three reflection types (sk_lsm_c003_0003) and the family of angles placement rule (sk_lsm_c003_0014). What is new here is the ORDER: diagnosis before placement. The chapter-3 material is not re-extracted.

the source states this is the thinking an experienced photographer performs on any arrangement, and that most of it becomes habitual and fast; the effort described is therefore an initial cost, not a per-shot cost

position the light, the subject, and the camera to capitalize on that reflection and minimize the others

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', sections 'Using an Opaque Black Background' and 'Using a Glossy Black Surface'
item.question: A matte black cosmetics compact has to be photographed on black, keeping detail in the product and a truly black ground. Black seamless paper is on hand. Walk through what this book says will happen and what to do.
item.answer: Black paper is one of the worst common choices, and the authors discuss it first only because it is usually the one available. The paper directly under the subject receives as much illumination as the subject, and since the compact has to be rendered dark grey rather than black to hold detail, the paper under it cannot be black either. A spotlight would keep the background darker but is ruled out, because producing direct reflection on the subject — which is how a black subject is rendered at all — requires a large source. Two things follow. First, replace the paper with a material producing less diffuse reflection than the subject: black velvet, at the same exposure, records far darker than the paper. Second, light the compact as if it were metal — find the family of angles and fill it. Velvet has two stated limits: a few subjects are so black that even velvet is not blacker, and the subject's edges may merge with its own shadow. For those edges the book offers glossy black acrylic and invisible light, at the cost that the overhead source then fills the acrylic's own family and the ground stops being black; the clean alternative is distance, putting the subject far enough from the background that lighting one does not touch the other.
item.support: Ch. 9, 'Lighting Black-on-Black Scenes' through 'Keeping the Subject Away from the Background', with the paper-versus-velvet pair at identical exposure.

using a spot or snoot to hold the background down, which the source rules out because the subject needs a large source

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Round Metal' and its three remedies
item.question: A polished sphere has to be photographed and the camera keeps appearing dead in the middle of it. Rank the book's three remedies and say what each actually achieves.
item.answer: First the constraint: the family of angles for round metal is practically the whole environment including the camera, the camera's reflection always falls exactly at the centre of the subject where it is most noticeable, and there are no view-camera tricks to move it out. So all three remedies are mitigations. Camouflage means any desirable clutter that makes the unwanted reflection less obvious — an irregular surface where the reflection can fall between the cracks, or additional subjects appropriate to the scene whose reflections break it up; the authors describe using ribbon and greenery this way on a department store catalogue cover. Keeping the light off the camera works because a camera in the dark cannot see itself reflected: confine the lighting to the subject, work farther away with a longer lens so less stray light falls on the camera, or cover it with black cloth or a black card with a hole — though that only works in a studio large enough that the surrounding walls do not reflect. A tent makes the environment and the source the same white enclosure, and the authors are candid that by itself it does not solve the problem: the dark camera hole and the tent seams reflect in the subject and must be retouched. Its value is that it makes the retouching easier.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'Round Metal' through 'Using a Tent', with the untented and tented ornament photographs.
confounders: expecting one of the three to remove the reflection outright; none does
building a larger tent to shrink the camera's reflection, which the source shows is always wasted
assuming a black-covered camera works anywhere; the source restricts it to a large studio

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', sections 'Using a Translucent White Background' and 'Using a Mirror Background'
item.question: Compare a translucent white background and a mirror background for a white-on-white subject, on the two things the book says each costs or gives.
item.answer: A translucent background lit from behind decouples subject and background entirely — with a reasonably opaque subject the background can be taken to any brightness without affecting the subject — and it costs the ground shadow, because light from beneath erases any hint of one. The authors then turn that cost into an advantage: because the shadow is now independent of the subject's lighting, it can be manufactured by tracing a pleasing test-light shadow onto paper, cutting it out and gluing the cut-out under the panel. A mirror is the easiest white background of all, because it reflects almost nothing but direct reflection and those reflections are much brighter than any diffuse white; a light large enough to fill the whole background's family of angles usually produces shadows soft enough that no fill is needed, and it is one of the few arrangements where the background reflects fill light under the subject. Its costs are that the light must show no texture, since it will be sharply reflected, that the subject's own reflection may be confusing depending on crop and shape, and that no ground shadow is obtainable at all.
item.support: Ch. 9, 'Using a Translucent White Background' and 'Using a Mirror Background', with the flower photographed on each.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Keeping the Metal Bright'; and 'Flat Metal'
item.question: A large fill light is added well outside the family of angles to lift a polished steel subject that is reading too dark. Nothing happens. Why, and what does that fact buy you elsewhere in the scene?
item.answer: Because polished metal produces almost no diffuse reflection, light coming from any angle other than inside the family of angles has practically no effect on it, regardless of how bright the light is or how long the exposure. The family is a hard boundary rather than a matter of degree. What that buys is the cleanest separation of controls in the book: everything outside the family acts only on the rest of the scene, so the metal's tone can be set entirely by what occupies the family while the background is set independently. It also produces a practical trap the authors flag: the large white target used to FIND the family must be removed before shooting dark metal, because left in place it reflects the general illumination and quietly becomes an additional source inside the family.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'Keeping the Metal Bright' for the statement about off-family light, 'Keeping the Metal Dark' for the test-surface warning. The spatula photographed from outside the family records as solid black on white paper.
confounders: adding more power, which the source says makes no difference
lengthening the exposure, which the source names explicitly as also making no difference
assuming a dulling-sprayed or brushed surface behaves the same way; adding diffuse reflection is exactly what breaks this

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', sections 'Keeping the Metal Bright', 'Keeping the Metal Dark' and 'The Elegant Compromise'
item.question: You are handed a brushed-steel flask and told it should read as a light mid-grey, sitting on a background that reads near-white, in one frame. Using only what this book gives you, how do you get both?
item.answer: Treat the two surfaces as reading different parts of the same source. The flask, being close to a pure direct reflector, responds only to whatever lies inside its family of angles; the background responds to the whole source through diffuse reflection. So one large soft source can serve both: the portion of it covering the family sets the flask's tone, and the whole of it sets the background's. Having more of the source inside the family makes the metal brighter; a source large enough that little of it falls inside makes the background brighter instead. Then use distance as the second control, since the background follows the inverse square law and the metal's direct reflection does not — moving the light closer lifts the background toward white while the flask holds its tone exactly. The book's phrase for this is the elegant compromise, and the claim worth taking from it is that the metal's tone is placeable at any step between black and white independently of the rest of the scene. The bound to watch is the lens: from a close viewpoint the family is wide and the source may only just fill it, in which case the light cannot be moved without the flask's edges going black.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'The Elegant Compromise' for the single-soft-box arrangement, 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light' for both the distance control and the lens bound. The matched spatula frames show the tonal independence directly.
confounders: using two lights and balancing their power, which works but misses that one large source already gives the control
expecting the metal to brighten when the light comes closer
ignoring the lens constraint, which is what makes the control fail from a close viewpoint

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.question: A brief calls for a steel component to read almost black in a soft, evenly lit scene. Simply putting the light near the camera does keep the metal dark and the authors reject the result. What is wrong with it, and what do they build instead?
item.answer: What is wrong is not the metal's tone but the shadows: the position of the soft shadows that arrangement produces does nothing to delineate the shape of the object, so the component reads dark and formless. The arrangement they build instead uses the marked family of angles directly. Assume the white target used to find the family was much larger than the minimum needed to fill it. Back the light up so it illuminates that entire diffusion sheet as evenly as possible, then attach a gobo cut to barely fill the family of angles. Every point of the sheet except the family lights the scene, so the light is large and soft while the metal stays black. Two practical notes: the white test target must be removed if it is not being used as the source, because left in place it would reflect the general illumination and act as an additional light; and the technique fails with an opaque white reflector card, because the light illuminating the card also illuminates the gobo, which then behaves more like a reflector than a blocker even if it is black — though the authors concede that hybrid might be the most pleasing compromise of all.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'Keeping the Metal Dark', including the removal of the test surface and the reflector-card failure condition.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', sections 'Photograph the Metal at an Angle' and 'Retouch the Reflection'
item.question: Two of the four remedies for a camera reflecting in flat metal are not lighting solutions at all. Compare them on the terms the book uses.
item.answer: Shooting the metal at an angle and correcting the geometry afterwards always results in some quality loss, and it requires composing with generous extra space because the trapezoidal projection has to be cropped to a rectangle; the authors call it a bad remedy that may be better than no remedy, to keep in mind if circumstances force it. Retouching the reflection out — shooting straight on, letting the camera reflect, and removing it afterwards — loses no image quality at all, and they say that for some subjects, especially large ones, it is so much easier than any lighting solution that it should not be forgotten. Their comparison is explicitly economic rather than optical: spending half a day lighting instead of half an hour at a computer makes no sense. They flag that it is not a lighting solution and decline to discuss it in detail, but they do not discourage it.

item.rationale: SPEC-01 lets an entity declare `allowed_variation: {lighting: true, viewing_angle: true}` alongside the invariants that constitute its identity. This source supplies a physical basis for setting those two flags per surface rather than per product. A matte surface's recorded brightness is independent of viewing angle, so its appearance is close to an identity property. A polished one's is not: what a mirror-like product shows is an image of its surroundings, so the same physical object legitimately looks different from a different angle or in a different room, and its centre will show whatever is in front of it. Declaring viewing_angle variation permissible for a brushed-metal tin and impermissible for a matte carton is a different decision, and the source says why.

source_terms: another good rule for black-on-black is to light it as if it were metal , regardless of the actual material
The best solution is to find a background material that produces less diffuse reflection than the subject. Black velvet serves this purpose
Much of the direct reflection from a black subject is likely to be polarized. If we use a polarizing filter to take the reflection off our table surface, we will probably turn the subject black too.
item.claim: Because a black subject's direct reflection has little diffuse competition, the rule for black-on-black is to capitalize on direct reflection wherever possible — in the source's words, to light it as if it were metal regardless of what it is actually made of, which means finding the family of angles and filling it. The background problem is then the hard part. Opaque black paper is the worst common choice: it receives as much light as the subject, and since the subject must be rendered dark grey rather than black to hold detail, the paper under it cannot be black either. A spotlight would keep the background darker but is ruled out, because the direct reflection wanted on the subject requires a large source. The source's answer is a background material producing less diffuse reflection than the subject — black velvet — with two stated limits: a few subjects are so black that even velvet is not blacker, and the subject's edges may merge with its own shadow. Glossy black acrylic supplies invisible light to fill those edges, but the same overhead source then fills the acrylic's family of angles and the background stops being black; the source argues its way to keeping this, saying the reflection under the subject is itself a sufficient clue that the surface is black and glossy, and concedes some readers will not accept that. The clean solution is distance: put the subject far enough from the background that lighting one does not touch the other. And the metal chapter's glass-support trick does not transfer — much of a black subject's direct reflection is polarized, so a polarizer used to clear the table would probably blacken the subject too.

mechanism.text: Black surfaces show direct reflection because their diffuse reflection is weak, which makes them behave for lighting purposes like polished metal. The glass-support trick depends on the subject and the support polarizing differently; black insulating subjects polarize like the glass, so the filter cannot discriminate.

item.rationale: Three inspections for any frame containing polished metal, each with a stated physical reason. First, is the metal reading as metal or as a grey card? Polished metal records at close to the brightness of whatever it reflects, so a metal surface sitting at a plausible mid grey across its whole area, with no bright region and no dark one, is showing the tonal signature of a diffuse surface rather than a mirror. Second, does the metal's edge separate from what it stands on? The source names the failure exactly — a near-pure direct reflector standing on its own light source records at the same brightness as that source, and the boundary disappears. Third, does the frame contain the source's own image? Because a direct reflection is a picture of the source, a shiny surface reports the size and shape of what lit it, and a hard-edged rectangle in a product's face is a legible artefact.

applicability.when: inspecting a frame containing polished or brushed metal, foil or another strongly direct-reflecting product surface
applicability.limits: Everything here is a statement about what a real camera records from real metal. Applying the three checks to a rendered frame is ours. The second check in particular assumes the depicted metal really is standing on the surface that appears to light it, which a generated image need not honour. Nothing about how to FIX any of these is bound outside bnd_lsmx_010: the source's answers are a light-toned background, a black card, a gobo, a polarizer or dulling spray, all physical.

item.claim: A camera placed square on to flat metal reflects in it. The source gives four remedies and is explicit about what each costs. A view camera or perspective-control lens is the best: the camera sits off-centre, outside the family of angles, with its back parallel to the subject so no perspective distortion is introduced, and the lens is shifted to re-centre the image — though a large shift may vignette the corners or reveal lens distortion, both minimised by working farther away with a longer lens. Shooting through a hole cut in the light source removes the camera's reflection but substitutes the hole's, which only works where the subject is irregular enough to camouflage it. Shooting at an angle and correcting in post always costs some image quality and requires composing loose enough to crop the trapezoid. Retouching the reflection out is not a lighting solution at all, but for some subjects it is so much cheaper than the lighting solutions that the source says it should not be forgotten, and it loses no quality.

mechanism.text: The camera lies inside the family of angles whenever it faces flat metal squarely; the remedies work either by moving the camera out of the family while keeping the image plane parallel, by concealing it inside the source, or by abandoning the geometric fix.

scope.conditions: flat metal that must appear centred and undistorted

caveats.text: the retouching recommendation is an economic judgement about a photographer's time, not an optical claim, and the source presents it as such

the source warns that lighting the area near the camera needs care in the hole-in-the-source arrangement: a light aimed at a reflector card can flare into the lens, and a light through a diffusion sheet can cast a shadow of the camera onto the sheet that then reflects visibly in the subject

item.rationale: SPEC-01 already assigns each entity a role, with `hero` among the permitted values. This source supplies a rule for filling that field in commercial work: the customer occupies the hero role and the brand occupies a supporting one. A brief that marks the product or the brand as hero and also claims to be customer-centric is a detectable conflict between two fields we already hold.

applicability.when: assigning entity roles for a brand asset intended to persuade a customer
applicability.limits: SPEC-01's `hero` marks the primary visual subject of an asset, while this source's hero is the protagonist of a narrative the customer is living. Those are not the same thing, and a product can be the visual subject of a shot in which the customer is still the protagonist. The rule is usable as a check on the message; it must not be read as forbidding product-led imagery.

source_terms: Whenever you can, make the product itself the hero of your advertising.
there are no dull products, only dull writers
item.claim: The product itself should be made the hero of the advertising wherever possible. The source rejects the excuse that a product is too dull, holding that there are no dull products only dull writers, and reports never assigning a product to a writer not personally interested in it, because every bad campaign the author wrote was for a product that did not interest him.

caveats.text: the source notes that showing the product with utter simplicity takes courage, because the writer will be accused of not being creative

source_stated_remedies: make the product itself the hero
do not assign a product to a writer who is not interested in it

source_terms: To build a quality brand you need to narrow the focus and combine that narrow focus with a better name and a higher price.
What can we put into our brand to justify the higher price?
item.claim: The authors' constructive prescription for quality perception has three components, and they state that the way to build it is to follow the other laws rather than to improve the product. Narrowing makes a brand a specialist, and specialists are perceived to know more; a better name beats an equal competitor with a worse one; a high price is itself a benefit, because it lets a buyer take public satisfaction from consumption. They invert the conventional order of design: instead of building quality and pricing to match, start with a higher price and then ask what can be put into the brand to justify it.

mechanism.text: Specialist perception is argued from the cardiologist against the general practitioner — most people believe the specialist knows more, and the authors say from a marketing point of view it does not matter whether that is true. High price works socially rather than functionally: the Rolex wearer is not buying punctuality but the public fact of affordability, and the authors ask whether $100 jeans would sell at that price with the label inside.

scope.conditions: the price move is offered specifically for 'a sea of similar products with similar prices'

caveats.text: the authors qualify their own advice: they say they always advise clients to build as much quality as they can afford, so this is a claim about what builds the brand, not a licence to build a worse product

the justification examples (a bigger and heavier watch, an oversized driver, a fatter pen, more butterfat, longer ageing) are product changes chosen after the brands succeeded; no case is given of the same tactic failing

source_stated_problems: conventional wisdom often advocates marketing a high-quality product at a comparable price
source_stated_remedies: deliberately start with a higher price

positive.description: brands the authors say benefit from high price, and the specific product changes used to justify the price in five of them

intra_source_relations.note: supplies the constructive half of the Law of Quality
narrow focus is one of the three components

item.claim: For a consideration objective, whose stated aim is to show users how the product fits into their lives, Attention is left at the core principles. Branding shifts to heroing the product. Connection carries two instructions, showing how the product works and being relatable. Direction is to plant the seed of urgency rather than to press for an immediate act.

scope.conditions: Campaigns whose marketing objective is consideration

caveats.text: "Hero the product" sits in the Branding column, so for this objective the source's branding instruction is about the product rather than about brand identity marks. The core Branding guideline already permits either, saying "your brand or product".
"Plant the seed of urgency" is a weaker ask than the action row's, and the difference between the two is the whole of the source's guidance on how directness should vary with objective.
No evidence is offered for this weighting. It is asserted in a table with no result attached to any cell.

Platform- and time-contingent. This is guidance about one company's ad products on one platform. Playback behaviour, ad formats and surfaces change; the source does not claim a durable mechanism and none should be read in.

Declared publisher interest. The publisher sells advertising on the platform whose creative guidance this is, and the cited research validates that product. Third-party involvement (Ipsos as research partner; Nielsen and Kantar as independent reviewers, per the source's own account) moderates this; it does not remove it.

intra_source_relations.note: urgency planted against the ask presented

source_terms: It pays to show the product being used, and, if possible, the end-result of using it.
In commercials for food, the more appetizing you make it look, the more you sell. It has been found that food in motion looks particularly appetizing.
It is a good thing to use close-ups when your product is the hero of your commercial. The closer you get on the candy bar, the more you make people's mouths water.
Mnemonics. This unpronounceable word is used to describe a visual device repeated over a long period.
item.claim: Showing the product in use pays, and where possible the end-result of using it — how a nappy keeps a baby dry, how pistons look after fifty thousand miles. For food the more appetising it looks the more it sells, and food in motion is said to look particularly appetising: chocolate sauce in the act of being poured, syrup over pancakes. Close-ups pay when the product is the hero of the commercial. Over a longer horizon he names mnemonics, a visual device repeated over a long period, which he says can increase brand identification and remind people of the promise.

scope.conditions: commercials where the product itself can be shown performing

caveats.text: none of these carries a measurement; 'it has been found' introduces the food-in-motion claim with nothing behind it
